replacement: [A company of mutinous Citizens enters, carrying staves, clubs, and other weapons.]
[Sicinius Velutus, Junius Brutus, two Tribunes; Cominius, Titus Lartius and other Senators enter.]
[Tullus Aufidius enters with Senators of Corioles.]
[Volumnia and Virgilia, mother and wife to Martius, enter. They sit down on two low stools and sew.]
[Valeria enters with an Usher and a Gentlewoman.]
[Martius and Titus Lartius enter, with drum and colours, with Captains and Soldiers, as before the city of Corioles. A Messenger comes to them.]
[Two Senators enter with others on the walls of Corioles.]
[The Volscian Army enters as through the city gates.]
[Alarums. The Romans are beaten back to their trenches. They exit, with the Volsces following.]
[Another alarum. The Volsces re-enter and are driven back to the gates of Corioles, which open to let them in.]
[Martius follows the fleeing Volsces through the gates, and is shut in.]
[Martius enters, bleeding, assaulted by the enemy.]
[They fight, and all enter the city.]
[Martius and Titus Lartius enter with a Trumpet.]

MARTIUS. Look at these scavengers, who value their hours at a cracked drachma. Cushions, lead spoons, irons worth a doit, the smallest coin, doublets that hangmen would bury with the men who wore them. These base slaves pack up their loot before the fight is even over. Down with them!
MARTIUS. May she be as much your friend as she is to those she places highest! So, farewell.
[Cominius enters as if in retreat, with Soldiers.]
COMINIUS. A shepherd can no more mistake thunder for a tabor than I can mistake the sound of Martius' voice for that of any lesser man.
[They all shout and wave their swords, lift him up in their arms, and cast up their caps.]
[Titus Lartius, having set a guard on Corioles, going with drum and trumpet toward Cominius and Caius Martius, enters with a Lieutenant, other Soldiers, and a Scout.]
[Alarum, as in battle. Martius and Aufidius enter at separate doors.]
[Here they fight, and certain Volsces come to the aid of Aufidius.]
[Martius fights till they are driven in breathless. Aufidius and Martius exit, separately.]
[Alarum. A retreat is sounded. Flourish. At one door, Cominius enters with the Romans; at another door, Martius, with his arm in a scarf.]
[Titus Lartius enters with his force, from the pursuit.]
[A long flourish. They all cry "Martius, Martius!" and cast up their caps and lances. Cominius and Lartius stand bare-headed.]
[A flourish. Cornets. Tullus Aufidius enters, bloody, with two or three soldiers.]
[Menenius enters with the two Tribunes of the people, Sicinius and Brutus.]
[He begins to exit. Brutus and Sicinius stand aside.]
[Cominius the General and Titus Lartius enter, between them Coriolanus crowned with an oak garland, with Captains and Soldiers and a Herald. Trumpets sound.]
[To Volumnia and Virgilia.] Your hand, and yours.
[Flourish of cornets. Exeunt in state, as before.]

SICINIUS. As you say, once this is suggested to them, at some moment when his soaring insolence offends the people, it will be his fire to light their dry stubble. That moment won't be lacking if it's pushed, and that's as easy as setting dogs on sheep. Their blaze will darken him forever.
[Two Officers enter, to lay cushions, as if in the Capitol.]

[A sennet. The Patricians and the Tribunes of the people enter, Lictors before them; Coriolanus, Menenius, Cominius the consul. The Patricians sit. Sicinius and Brutus take their places by themselves. Coriolanus stands.]
[Coriolanus rises, and tries to go away.]
[Flourish of cornets. Exeunt all but Sicinius and Brutus.]
[Coriolanus enters in a gown of humility, with Menenius.]

SICINIUS. Let them assemble and, on safer judgment, all revoke your ignorant election. Stress his pride and his old hatred of you. Also, don't forget with what contempt he wore the humble gown, and how he scorned you in his request. But your love, thinking of his services, took from you any grasp of how he was acting then. He did it most mockingly and without dignity, shaped by the old hatred he bears you.
[Cornets. Coriolanus, Menenius, all the gentry, Cominius, Titus Lartius and other Senators enter.]

CORIOLANUS. "Shall"? Oh, good but most unwise patricians! You grave but reckless senators, have you let the Hydra, the many-headed monster, choose an officer for itself? He is only the horn and the noise of the monster, yet with his commanding "shall" he has the nerve to say he'll turn your river into a ditch and make your channel his own. If he has power, then lower your heads in shame at your ignorance. If he has none, wake up from your dangerous softness. If you are wise, don't act like common fools. If you are not, let them have cushions beside you. You are plebeians if they are senators. And they are no less than that when your votes and theirs are blended, and the strongest flavor is theirs. They choose their magistrate, and he is the kind of man who sets his "shall," his popular "shall," against a more serious bench than ever frowned in Greece. By Jove himself, it makes the consuls look base! And my soul aches to think how soon, when two authorities are up and neither is supreme, confusion may enter the gap between them and make one swallow the other.
[A rabble of Plebeians enter with the Aediles.]
Tribunes, patricians, citizens — what, ho! Sicinius, Brutus, Coriolanus, citizens!
[In this mutiny the Tribunes, the Aediles and the People are beaten back.]
[Brutus and Sicinius enter again with the rabble.]

MENENIUS. Oh, he's a limb that has only a disease. Cutting it off would be deadly, but curing it is easy. What has he done to Rome that deserves death? He killed our enemies. The blood he has lost, and I dare swear it is many an ounce more than what he has left, he spilled for his country. And to have what is left lost at his own country's hands would be, for all of us who do it and allow it, a brand of shame until the end of the world.

VOLUMNIA. Please now, my son, go to them with this cap in your hand. Hold it out as far as this, and here stand before them, with your knee kissing the stones. In such business action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant are more learned than their ears. Wave your head, which often corrects your stout heart this way, and be humble now, like the ripest mulberry that won't bear handling. Or say to them that you are their soldier, bred in battles, and you lack the soft manner that you admit would suit you to use, as they have a right to claim it, when asking for their good love. But say that from now on you will, in truth, make yourself theirs, as far as you have power and person.
[Coriolanus, Menenius and Cominius enter with other Senators.]
[Coriolanus and Cominius exit with the other Senators.]
[They all shout and throw up their caps.]
[Coriolanus, Volumnia, Virgilia, Menenius, Cominius enter with the young nobility of Rome.]
[The two Tribunes, Sicinius and Brutus, enter with the Aedile.]
VOLSCIAN. It is, sir. Truly, I've forgotten you.
ROMAN. I am a Roman, but I serve against Rome, just as you do. Do you know me yet?
VOLSCIAN. You had more beard when I last saw you, but your voice proves who you are. What's the news in Rome? I have orders from the Volscian state to find you there. You've saved me a day's journey.
VOLSCIAN. There have been? Is it over, then? Our state doesn't think so. They're making ready for war, and they hope to attack the Romans while they're still burning with their divisions.
VOLSCIAN. You'll be welcome with this news, Nicanor.
VOLSCIAN. He can't fail. I'm very lucky to run into you like this. You've finished my errand, and I'll gladly travel home with you.
VOLSCIAN. A magnificent one. The centurions and their companies are separately quartered, already on pay, and ready to march within an hour's warning.
VOLSCIAN. You take the words out of my mouth, sir. I have the most reason to be glad of yours.
[Coriolanus enters in mean apparel, disguised and muffled.]
[The Third Servingman enters; the First, coming in, meets him.]
[The two Tribunes, Sicinius and Brutus, enter.]
COMINIUS. You have helped to rape your own daughters, to have the city's lead roofs melted down on your heads, and to see your wives dishonored right under your noses —
MENENIUS. Please now, your news? You have done fine work, I fear. Please, your news? If Martius should be joined with the Volscians —

AUFIDIUS. I can't help it now, unless by taking action I cripple the foot of our whole plan. He carries himself more proudly, even toward me, than I thought he would when I first embraced him. Yet his nature never changes in that, and I must excuse what can't be mended.
[Menenius, Cominius, Sicinius, Brutus (the two Tribunes), and others enter.]
[Menenius enters and approaches the Watch, or Guard.]
[Virgilia, Volumnia, Valeria, young Martius enter with attendants.]
[He holds her by the hand, silent.]

MENENIUS. So he did me, and he remembers his mother no more now than an eight-year-old horse does. The sourness of his face turns ripe grapes sour. When he walks, he moves like a siege engine, and the ground shrinks under his tread. He can pierce a breastplate with his eye, talks like a funeral bell, and his hum is a cannonade. He sits on his throne like something made for Alexander. What he orders to be done is finished as soon as he orders it. He lacks nothing of a god but eternity and a heaven to sit enthroned in.
[Two Senators enter, with the Ladies (Volumnia, Virgilia, Valeria) passing over the stage, along with other Lords.]
THIRD CONSPIRATOR. Sir, his stubbornness when he stood for consul, which he lost for lack of stooping —
FIRST CONSPIRATOR. So he did, my lord. The army marveled at it. And in the end, when he had carried Rome and we expected no less spoil than glory —
[Drums and trumpets sound, with great shouts from the people.]
[Coriolanus enters marching with Drum and Colours, the Commoners being with him.]
[The Conspirators draw, and kill Martius, who falls. Aufidius stands on him.]
[They exit, bearing the body of Martius. A dead march sounds.]
